introduction: The Food and Nutrition School-Based Assessment combines research and practical work: you choose a theme, gather background information, plan and prepare meals that demonstrate what you have learned, and evaluate the results. Marks are given for the quality of your research, the plan, the preparation and presentation of the food, safety and hygiene, the nutritional or cost justification, and your honest evaluation. Check the current CSEC syllabus and your teacher's guidance for the exact requirements and number of practical sessions for your year.

tasks.title: Theme and background
tasks.explanation: State your theme (for example meals for a hypertensive adult, reducing food waste, or value-added use of local produce), and explain why it matters. Show evidence of research from books, articles or an interview.

tasks.title: Menus and costing
tasks.explanation: Write out the menu or menus with standard recipes, the number of portions, the cost per portion, and the reasons for each food choice in relation to your theme.

tasks.title: Time plan
tasks.explanation: Prepare a time plan sequencing all tasks from shopping to service, showing the order of work, the equipment and the time for each step.

tasks.title: Preparation and presentation
tasks.explanation: Carry out the preparation and cooking safely and hygienically, manage time and equipment, and present the finished dishes attractively and at the correct temperature.

tasks.title: Judgement and improvements
tasks.explanation: Evaluate the dishes by sensory properties and against your theme, compare plan with practice, discuss problems such as timing, cost or texture, and recommend specific improvements.

tasks.title: What you learned
tasks.explanation: Summarise what the assignment showed about nutrition, food management or food science, and how you would apply it.

sampleTitle: Meals for a household with a hypertensive adult, prepared on a weekly food budget

sample.body: Menu: steamed fish with herbs, lime and pepper; roasted breadfruit; steamed callaloo; sliced tomato and cucumber; fresh orange juice, no added sugar. Cost per portion: fish $180, breadfruit $60, callaloo $40, salad $35, juice $30 - total $345 per portion, against a budget of $400. Salt is omitted and flavour supplied by garlic, ginger, lime, pepper and scallion, since the theme requires a low-sodium diet.
sample.tips: State the cost per portion and justify each choice against the theme - this is where the nutrition marks are earned.

sample.body: The dish was attractive and evenly cooked, and the fish was moist although it was steamed five minutes longer than planned because two pieces were thick. Steaming preserved the vitamin C in the callaloo better than boiling would have, and omitting salt was accepted by the family once the herbs and lime were added. The juice was prepared last so it did not lose vitamin C before serving. Improvement: cut the fish into even portions next time and start the breadfruit earlier, because it delayed service by ten minutes.
sample.tips: Compare plan with practice, name specific problems and give specific remedies.

marking: Marks reward relevant research, sound menu planning with costing, a complete and realistic time plan, good practical skill with safe and hygienic working, attractive presentation, and a thoughtful evaluation with recommendations.

categories.comment: The theme comes out of the household's own kitchen and is answered with real work: the clinic's advice and the household's own target are written down, the salt pack is weighed at the start and the end of the week, the seasoning cubes are counted, twelve pack labels are read and turned into portion figures, the chicken is priced in three shops and the household's own receipts set the budget - and the folder says plainly that it is a school project and not medical advice.

The seven-day menu follows five written rules, every recipe carries its quantities for four portions, its technique and the reason for it, the market list is priced line by line against the five heads of the budget, and the practical dinner is costed against the dinner it replaced at J$2,133.86 against J$2,044.50 - with the difference explained rather than hidden. The plan and the costing agree to the cent, and the budget is checked before the shopping is done.

The time plan orders twelve stages from the hand wash to the washing up, with the equipment for each and the reason for the order, and it is run against the clock: 155 minutes planned, 168 taken, 13 over and still inside the 165 minutes allowed. Every overrun is traced to its real cause - a sandy bunch of callaloo, a large pumpkin, two scales that disagreed by 5 g in 500 g - and the three stages that came in early are named as well.

Hygiene and safety are planned rather than assumed: raw chicken on its own board, the chicken taken to 78 degrees C in the thigh with the probe swabbed before and after, the callaloo washed until the third water is clear, the panellists asked about allergies, and the food carried home above 60 degrees C. Every ingredient is weighed in and weighed out, the four portions are weighed within 15 g of each other, and the sodium, energy, protein, potassium and fibre of the plate are worked out ingredient by ingredient from the food tables.

The evaluation is candid about what failed: three of the seven days miss the household's own 1,500 mg target, the counting method is shown to leave out 195.8 mg a portion of sodium naturally in the food, the salted fish is named as an assumption and not a measurement, and the reworked dinner is admitted to be dearer than the meal it replaced. It then works out the three changes that close the gap - 1,478 mg a day with fresh fish in place of salted, 1,383 with the ketchup off the table, 1,283 with a packed lunch on the sports day - and the blind panel's scores settle the taste question with 11 of 12 choosing the new gravy.

The conclusion answers the aim in figures the folder has already established - the sodium for each person fell from 3,982.1 mg a day to 1,693.2 on a method that under-counts, and the week cost J$23,989.00 of the J$25,300.00 set aside - states where the plan fails as clearly as where it works, names the two habits the household kept, and says what a second attempt would do differently.

The household is my own family, the Reids of Sample Village: my father Mr Delroy Reid, 52 (invented), who drives a taxi and was told at the clinic three years ago that his blood pressure was high and that he had to cut down on salt; my mother Mrs Pauline Reid, 48 (invented), who does the shopping and keeps the money; my brother Ricardo, 14 (invented); and me, 16, in Form 5, who cooks on evenings and at weekends. The household, the shops, the prices, the panel and every figure in this folder are invented for this worked example, and the folder is a school assignment and not medical advice. What I set out to do was to plan one whole week of family meals, cost the week against the money the family can actually set aside, cook one of the dinners in the school laboratory and have it tasted blind against the seasoned, salty dinner it replaced. The folder has 25 sections: the research into the household and into what the family used to eat, the labels read in the cupboard, the shop survey and the budget; the aim, the hypothesis and the variables; the plan, the recipes, the market list, the costing and the time plan; the record of the practical session itself; the results, table by table, for the sodium, the money, the time and the taste; and the discussion, the limitations and the conclusion. Every figure comes from one set of weights and prices, so the numbers in one table agree with the numbers in the next.

pages.heading: Research: the household, the household's health and how the theme was chosen
pages.body: The theme came out of the kitchen, not out of a book. Three years ago my father was told at the health centre that his blood pressure was too high. He was given tablets and told to cut down on salt, and he was told that the salt in the cooking was the part he could most easily change. He is 52, he drives a taxi for ten hours a day and he eats at home for breakfast and at night, with one lunch bought on the road. He does not smoke and he is not overweight. My mother does the shopping and keeps the money, and she was the one who said the food would taste flat if the salt came out, so the argument I wanted to settle with this project was whether a week of family food could be cooked with far less salt, still be eaten without complaint, and cost no more than the week the family was already paying for. That is the whole theme: meals for a household with a hypertensive adult, prepared on a weekly food budget. The household's own working target came from the clinic's advice rather than from me: the family agreed to keep my father's day below 1,500 mg of sodium, which is below the figure the World Health Organization gives for adults (less than 5 g of salt, about 2,000 mg of sodium, a day). The doctor's advice was about salt and not about the rest of the plan, and the family showed the plan to the clinic nurse before the week started; nothing in this folder is medical advice to anybody else, and a person with kidney disease in particular must not copy a plan that pushes the fruit, peas and green vegetables up without asking first. The household is four people: two adults, one teenager and me. My father eats what everybody eats, so the plan had to work for the household, not for him alone on a separate plate - a point my mother made in the first conversation and the reason there is no 'special food' anywhere in this folder.

pages.heading: Research: what the family ate before and how much salt went into it
pages.body: The first job was to find out how much salt the household was really using, because asking my mother would only have produced a guess. On the Sunday before the project I opened a new 500 g pack of salt, weighed it, put it in the kitchen and told everybody it was the salt for the week; the next Sunday I weighed it again and 144 g had gone, which is about 20.6 g of salt a day for the whole household's cooking. A level teaspoon of salt is about 6 g, so the household was putting about 3.4 level teaspoons of salt a day into the pots of food for four people, and that is before anything added at the table. The seasoning cubes were counted the same way: a pack of 20 cubes (J$1,200.00) was replaced about three weeks later, so about one cube a day was going into the pot. The other half of the picture is the goods that carry a label. My mother kept the shopping receipts for the week before the project, and I wrote down what each person ate from the goods with a label on them - the bread, the margarine, the ketchup, the milk, the tinned mackerel and corned beef, the patties on the days a lunch was bought on the road, and the salted fish on Sunday morning. The table adds the three parts together for the same seven days: salt in the pots (14,400.0 mg for each of us across the week, which is 2,057.1 mg a day), the seasoning cubes, and the labelled goods. The result is a household average of 3,982.1 mg of sodium a person a day, and the honest reading of that figure is that the family's usual week was running at about double the World Health Organization figure for adults. Sunday is the worst day in the table at 6,025 mg, and that is the ackee and salted fish: the pack label for salted cod gives 8,000 mg of sodium in 100 g as it is sold, and even counted at half, to allow for the soaking and the boiling, a 60 g portion is 2,400 mg by itself. That one dish explains why Sunday stands out, and it is the dish the household is least willing to give up, which is what makes it worth the whole project.

pages.heading: Research: reading the labels in the cupboard
pages.body: Once the salt tin had been weighed, the next job was the goods that nobody thinks of as salty. I emptied the cupboard and the fridge onto the table and read every label, writing down the sodium figure the label gives and the figure it works out to for the amount we actually eat at one time. This is the part of the research that changed the plan most. Everybody in the household knew about the salt in the pot, because it comes out of a pack you can see going down; almost nobody realised that the seasoning cube puts 275 mg of sodium into each person's plate, that a 15 g spoon of ketchup puts in 165 mg, or that the browning brushed on the chicken carries sodium of its own. Reading the labels turned four items in the cupboard into decisions: the cube and the corned beef came out of the basket altogether, the ketchup came off the table after the first week, and the browning and the salted fish were halved rather than dropped, because the household wanted the colour of the chicken and the taste of the Sunday breakfast. Two things I want to say honestly about this table. The first is that a label gives sodium and not salt: multiplying the sodium in a portion by 2.5 gives about the salt, so the 1,600 mg counted for the Sunday saltfish is about 4 g of salt, which is a whole day's salt in one breakfast dish. The second is the assumption in the salted fish row: the label is for the fish as it is sold, and soaking and boiling take some of the salt out, but we did not send a sample to a laboratory and we could not measure how much. Counting it at half is a working assumption, it is written down as one, and the whole Sunday figure is sensitive to it; the folder comes back to that point in the limitations.

pages.heading: Research: what the three shops charge and why the market came out cheaper
pages.body: The same Saturday morning I priced the chicken at the three places this household can reach: the market in Sample Village, the poultry shop on the riverside, and the supermarket on the main road. I priced the same weight in each place - the 4.2 kg of chicken a week the plan needs for four people - so that the three shops were compared on what the week actually costs and not on a price a pound read off a board. The market won for two reasons that both matter to this project. The first is money: buying whole birds and jointing them at home costs J$3,990.00 for the week against J$5,250.00 for the supermarket's ready-seasoned parts, a saving of J$1,260.00 on the week's chicken alone, which is 5 per cent of the whole weekly food budget. The second reason matters more for the sodium: the supermarket's parts come already seasoned, and when we asked, the seasoning on them is salt-based; the parts are also dearer for the same meat. Buying the whole bird means the seasoning on the chicken is the seasoning I put on it and weigh myself, which is the only way the 1 g of salt in the recipe means anything. The third reason is the bones: the carcass and the wing tips from four birds make about two litres of stock for the rice and the soup, so part of what the market saves in money comes back as flavour in the pot. The prices in this table are the invented prices used throughout this folder; the same price list is applied to the market list, to the practical dinner and to the week the household spent before the project, so the comparisons hold together.

pages.heading: Research: the weekly food budget and how it was set
pages.body: A plan that costs more than the household has is not a plan, so the money came before the menu. My mother keeps the shopping receipts, and she worked out from them that the family had been spending J$26,892.28 a week on food, which is J$1,592.28 more than the household wants to spend. The household agreed to set J$25,300.00 aside for food and drink for the week, and my mother split it into the five heads in the table below before any menu was written, so that the menu had to fit the money rather than the other way round. Each head is a rule and not a guess: the meat and fish head is what the household can afford for protein, the peas and staples head carries the rice, the peas and the oil, and the vegetables and fruit head is the biggest in the budget on purpose, because the plan leans on vegetables and fruit to do the work the salt used to do. The figure in the last column is what the head works out to for each of the four of us for a day, and it is worth reading it as it stands: J$903.57 a person a day, which is the real constraint on this project. My mother's own comment on the budget was that the vegetables were never the problem - the tinned meat, the patties bought at school and the sweet drinks were; the table in section 20 comes back to that and shows whether she was right. The budget is also the reason the plan buys one bird at a time rather than a week's meat in one trip: buying smaller quantities at the market on the way home keeps the money in the house and the meat out of the freezer, where the family has lost food before.

pages.heading: Design: the aim, the hypothesis and the variables
pages.body: The aim of the project is to plan, cost and cook a week of family meals for a household of four that includes a hypertensive adult, keeping the sodium in the day as low as the household can manage without the food being refused, and to find out whether the meals the family likes can still be cooked without the salt they were used to. Two smaller aims sit inside that one: to find out what the week costs against the money the household can set aside, and to find out whether a panel of ordinary eaters can tell the difference between the seasoned gravy the household used to make and the new one. The hypothesis is this: if the salt in the cooking is cut from about 20.6 g a day to about 5.7 g a day for the household, and the seasoning cubes, the corned beef, the pre-seasoned chicken and the ketchup are dropped or cut, while garlic, ginger, pimento, thyme, escallion, black pepper and lime are used to carry the flavour, then the sodium in each person's day will fall by more than half, the family will still eat the food, and the week will cost no more than J$25,300.00. Each part of that hypothesis can be measured: the salt was weighed, the labels were read, the food was weighed, the money was receipted and the taste was scored by a panel. The variables table sets out what was changed on purpose and what had to be held still, and the last row is the honest one: two things could not be held still at all. The season of the year changed the price of tomato and sweet pepper between the survey and the shopping trip, and the family still eats one lunch a day away from home, which the plan can allow for but cannot control.

pages.heading: Method: how the project was organised and the session was run
pages.body: The project ran over three weeks. In the first week I talked to the household, weighed the salt, counted the cubes, read every label and priced the chicken in the three shops. In the second week I planned the menu, wrote the recipes, built the market list and costed it against the budget, weighed the salt pack again at the end of that week and wrote the time plan for the practical. In the third week the household cooked and ate the seven-day plan at home, and I cooked the practical dinner in the school laboratory in one session of 165 minutes, which is what the teacher allowed. The practical session is the part I have to describe most carefully, because most of the results come out of it. The ingredients were weighed at home the morning of the session on the kitchen scale, written on the plan sheet and carried to school in labelled containers, so that the school scales were only used to check them; that was a deliberate choice, because the two school scales were found to differ from each other by 5 g in a 500 g bag of rice. In the laboratory I cooked the dinner for four portions: the baked chicken, the brown rice and pigeon peas, the steamed callaloo, the pumpkin and carrot, and the pawpaw with yoghurt. The four portions were plated and weighed, the serving temperature was taken, and the panellists tasted in the room next door while the food was hot. For the blind tasting I made two gravies from the same base - the pan juices of the same batch of chicken, brought up to one litre each with water - and seasoned one the household's usual way and one the new way, so that the seasoning was the only difference between them. The two gravies went into identical flasks marked only A and B by my teacher, and the panel of twelve (my classmates, invented, plus the teacher) tasted 10 ml of each from coded cups with water between them, without being told which was which. The remaining three portions were packed hot into clean covered containers, carried home in an insulated bag in the 25 minutes it takes to walk from the school, and eaten by the household within 90 minutes of being cooked; the fourth portion was the one the panel tasted, and what was left of it was not kept. The record was kept in a book on the kitchen table: every weight, every time, every temperature and every score went in as it happened rather than being remembered afterwards.

pages.heading: Planning: the seven-day menu and the salt allowed each day
pages.body: The menu was written to five rules the household agreed before I started. Fruit every day. A dark green vegetable and a yellow or orange vegetable or fruit every day, because the colours are where the potassium and the vitamin A are and because a plate with three colours on it does not look like a smaller meal. Peas or beans three times in the week and fish twice, so that the chicken is not carrying the whole week. No seasoning cube anywhere. The salt is weighed with the 1 g spoon and written into the pot, not poured, and there is no salt cellar on the table. The plan puts about 5.7 g of salt a day into the household's cooking, which is 40 g for the week and about 1.4 g for each person a day - a little under a quarter of a teaspoon each - and every one of those grams is in the last column of the table, added up day by day. Writing the salt down as a line in the menu, rather than adding it as you cook, is what makes the plan checkable: the salt tin was weighed at the start and the end of the week and 40 g had gone, which is exactly what the menu says. The menu is also where the money discipline lives. Nothing appears twice on a day if it can be cooked once and eaten twice: Saturday's pumpkin soup is Sunday's lunch, and the chicken on Sunday night is Monday's lunch in the bread. That is how a plan that puts more vegetables and fruit on the table than the household used to eat still fits inside the budget in section 6 - the money is moved out of the tinned meat and the patties and into the market.

pages.heading: Planning: the recipes, the quantities and the techniques
pages.body: Every recipe the household cooked during the planned week was written out with its quantities for four portions, the technique to be used and the reason for that technique, before the week started. Writing the reason down beside the technique turned out to matter more than I expected: it is the place where the plan argues with itself. The callaloo is steamed and drained rather than boiled in salted water because water takes the potassium out of the leaf as well as any salt in it; the salt in the vegetables is added last, off the heat, so that it is tasted on the food rather than dissolved away in the cooking water; the browning is brushed on rather than poured because the label shows it carries sodium; and the chicken keeps its bones because a bone-in piece baked in a covered tray stays moist without fat. The recipes below are the ones that were actually used, and the quantities are the ones weighed at home on the morning of the practical, not the quantities remembered afterwards. The last two rows are the comparison the panel tastes: two litres of gravy from the same base chicken, one seasoned the way the household used to season it and one seasoned the new way. That pair of recipes is the reason the results in section 18 can be read as a comparison at all, because everything except the seasoning is held still.

pages.heading: Planning: the market list for the week against the budget
pages.body: The market list was built from the recipes backwards: I wrote down everything the seven-day menu needed, priced every line from the price list used throughout this folder, and then added it up and checked it against the five heads of the budget from section 6 before going near a shop. The list came to J$23,989.00 against the J$25,300.00 the household set, which leaves J$1,311.00 or 5.2 per cent of the budget unspent. Every one of the five heads came in under its own figure as well, which was not an accident: when the first version of the list went over on the bread, milk and margarine head, the cheese was moved to two days a week and the milk was kept at the 200 ml a person a day the porridge needs, and the head came back under. Two decisions in this list are worth pointing at because they are where the money for the vegetables came from. The first is the chicken: four whole birds bought at the market and jointed at home, at J$950.00 a kg, instead of the ready-cut and seasoned parts at J$1,250.00 a kg, which is the saving worked out in section 5. The second is what is not on the list at all: no seasoning cubes, no corned beef, no sweet drinks and no biscuits. Those four lines alone are the difference between the week the household used to have and the week it now plans, and the comparison is set out in section 20. The peas and the staples head is the one to watch in a household that eats chicken three times a week: the pigeon peas at J$600.00 a kg are the dearest thing in that head, and the plan uses fresh peas once and dried red peas twice, which brings the head in under its figure.

pages.heading: Planning: what the practical dinner cost and the meal it replaced
pages.body: The dinner the practical session replaced is the household's own Sunday dinner, cooked the way my mother cooked it before the project: 1,400 g of ready-cut, seasoned chicken for four, white rice, and a pot seasoned with 12 g of salt, one seasoning cube, 10 ml of browning and a spoon of ketchup. Costing the two dinners side by side was the most uncomfortable piece of arithmetic in the whole project, because the honest answer is that the reworked dinner costs more: J$2,133.86 for four portions against J$2,044.50, which is J$89.36 more, or J$22.34 more for each of us. The chicken went down by J$895.00 because there is 500 g less of it and it was bought as a whole bird, and the seasoning went down by J$80.14 because the cube and the ketchup are gone, but the vegetables and fruit went up by J$722.50 and the peas by J$178.00, and together they more than cover the saving. Two things make that easier to accept, and I want them written down rather than argued away. The first is that the week as a whole does come in under the budget, because the dinner is not the only meal: the tinned meat, the patties, the sweet drinks and the biscuits that left the basket pay for the vegetables and the fruit several times over, and section 20 shows that the whole week costs J$2,903.28 less than the week the household spent before the project. The second is what the extra money buys on the plate: this dinner carries 558.3 mg of sodium for each of us against 1,900.0 mg in the meal it replaced, and it carries the peas, the callaloo, the pumpkin, the carrot and the fruit that the usual dinner did not have at all. The comparison is worth reading as a trade rather than as a win: J$22.34 more on the plate for about 1,341.7 mg less sodium, and that is the trade the household has to be willing to make every day for the plan to work.

pages.heading: Planning: the time plan and the order of work
pages.body: The time plan was written in the order the work had to happen, with the reason for the order built into it rather than added afterwards. The chicken is seasoned before anything else because it wants to stand for half an hour; the oven is loaded second so that it bakes while the vegetables are prepared, which is the only reason a dinner of five dishes fits into one session; the callaloo is washed before the pumpkin is peeled because the washing water has to be thrown away and the board has to be cleaned before the root vegetables are cut on it. The whole plan came to 155 minutes and the session took 168, which is 13 minutes or 8.4 per cent over the plan and inside the 165 minutes the teacher allowed, so the dinner was served on time even though the plan was missed. The overrun is worth reading stage by stage. 6 of the twelve stages ran over and 3 came in under the plan, and the largest single overrun is stage 4, preparing the vegetables, at 5 minutes: the callaloo was sandy and needed four washes instead of three, and the pumpkin was larger than the one weighed at the market, so it took longer to peel. That is a planning mistake and not bad luck: the callaloo was bought loose at the market without looking at the soil on it, and the pumpkin was chosen for size rather than weighed against the recipe. The next largest overruns are the weighing (stage 2) and the chicken (stage 6), and both have a real cause the folder records: the two school scales differed by 5 g in a 500 g bag of rice, so every weight was taken twice; and the chicken pieces were larger than the ones the recipe was written for, so the temperature was checked twice and the tray came out 4 minutes later. The three stages that came in under the plan were the callaloo steaming, the pumpkin and carrot, and the panel preparations, and in each case the saving came from something done earlier or already at home: the cups were coded the night before, and the callaloo was already cut small from the washing stage. If the plan were written again, the 5 minutes gained at stage 7 and the 2 minutes at stage 10 would be moved into the vegetable preparation at stage 4, where the time was actually needed.

pages.heading: Method: hygiene, safety, equipment and the keeping of the food
pages.body: The practical session was cooked in the school laboratory with the teacher in the room, and the hygiene and safety rules were the ones the class uses, written into the plan rather than remembered on the day. Raw chicken is the food in this dinner with the most to answer for, so it was handled first, on its own board, with its own knife and its own bowl, and everything it touched was washed in hot soapy water before any vegetable was cut. The chicken reached 78 degrees C in the thickest part of the thigh, which is above the 74 degrees C the textbook gives for poultry, and the probe was wiped with an alcohol swab before and after it was used, because a probe pushed into raw meat and then into cooked meat carries bacteria with it. The callaloo was washed three times in running water and the third wash was clear, which is the test the class uses for leafy greens. The bench was sanitised at the start and again between the raw chicken and the vegetables. On the panel side, the twelve panellists were asked about allergies before tasting and told what was in the two cups and the plate - chicken, peas, rice, vegetables, lime, yoghurt and dairy milk - and the cups and spoons were washed and dried before use, with a clean cup for each panellist and a fresh jug of water for the mouth between the two cups. Nobody dipped a spoon back into a cup, and the panel's portions were not returned to the serving dishes. The food that was not tasted was packed hot, straight from the pot, into clean covered containers, carried in an insulated bag and eaten within 90 minutes, which keeps it inside the two hours the class rule gives for hot food; nothing was left standing on the bench, and the containers were washed at home the same night. Nothing in this plan involves a hot fat or a pressure cooker, which were not needed, and the one piece of equipment that could burn anybody - the oven tray - was moved with dry cloths and put on the hob, not on the bench. The kitchen at home was run to the same rules, with the salt spoon kept in the salt tin so that no one helped themselves by hand.

Every weight in the first two columns was taken on the kitchen scale, the bought weight at home in the morning and the served weight after cooking and draining, and the difference between the two columns is worth reading because it shows where the food went. The two biggest changes are both water: the brown rice gained 360 g as it took up the cooking water, and the callaloo lost 100 g when the stalks and the cooking water came off it. The table is also the check on the portions. The dinner produced 764 g of food and 59 ml of yoghurt and oil for each of the four of us, plated and weighed, and the four plates were within 15 g of each other before the service spoons went out, which is the point of weighing rather than serving by eye: it is the only way to know that my father's plate carried the same sodium as everybody else's, because the plan is a household plan and there is no separate plate for him. pages.heading: Practical results: the sodium in the cooked dinner, ingredient by ingredient
pages.body: For this one dinner every ingredient was weighed and its sodium worked out from the food tables or from the label on the pack, so this is the only meal in the folder where the sodium is measured rather than counted. The pot came to 2,233.1 mg of sodium altogether, which is 558.3 mg for each of us. Two rows in that total deserve naming. The first is the salt: 3 g weighed with the 1 g spoon puts 1,200 mg into the pot, which is 300 mg each, and it is still the largest single item in the dinner even after being cut from 12 g to 3 g. The second is the sodium that was in the food before anything was added: 783.1 mg, or 195.8 mg each, from the chicken, the callaloo, the carrot, the pawpaw and the yoghurt. That second figure is the honest limitation of the household's day-to-day counting method, and it is the reason this dinner is counted two ways in the table: by the method the household can actually use every day - the weighed salt and the label figures, 362.5 mg each - and by the full measurement, 558.3 mg each. The difference is 195.8 mg a portion, and it is the size of the blind spot in the seven-day table that follows. The comparison with the meal this dinner replaced is the other result worth carrying forward: the household's usual pot held 7,600.0 mg of sodium for the same four people, or 1,900.0 mg each, so the reworked dinner is down by 1,341.7 mg a portion, a fall of 70.6 per cent. Both dinners are the same size, cooked in the same kitchen for the same four people, and the food tables were used for both, so the comparison is like for like.

pages.body: This is the table the household can keep using after the project, because it counts only the two things anybody can count in a kitchen: the salt that goes into the pot, weighed, and the sodium printed on the label of anything that has a label. The week came to 11,852.5 mg of sodium for each of us, an average of 1,693.2 mg a day, which is 57.5 per cent lower than the 3,982.1 mg a day the household was running at before the project. Against the household's own working target of 1,500 mg for my father, 3 of the seven days came in over and four came in well under. The days that went over are easy to name, and naming them is the point of the table. Friday went over because of the cheese; Saturday because of the patty bought at the sports day, which alone is 700 mg; and Sunday, far ahead of both, because of the salted fish on Sunday morning, a single dish of 1,600 mg counted at half the label figure. There is no way to be honest about this table without saying that Sunday is the day the plan does not reach its target, and that the household knew it before the week started, because the ackee and saltfish is the one meal nobody wanted to give up. Two figures sit underneath this table and have to be said out loud rather than hidden in a footnote. The first is that the counting method leaves out the sodium that fresh food carries by itself; section 16 measured it at 195.8 mg a portion for the practical dinner, so Wednesday - which this table puts at 1,292.5 mg - is really at least 1,488.3 mg when the dinner is counted ingredient by ingredient, and would be higher again if every meal of the day were counted the same way. The second is that the salt tin backs the table up: 40 g of salt went out of the kitchen in the planned week, which is exactly what the menu says, so the first column of this table is measured and not estimated. The table is, in the end, a floor rather than a ceiling: the household's real intake is a little above these figures, and it was still far below the week it started from.

pages.heading: Practical results: the blind tasting of the two gravies
pages.body: The tasting was the part of the project I was least sure about, because my father is not a trained taster and neither are my classmates. Two litres of gravy were made from the same base chicken - the pan juices brought up to a litre each with water - and one was seasoned the household's usual way, with 12 g of salt and a seasoning cube, and the other the new way, with 3 g of salt and the herbs. The usual litre carries 590 mg of sodium in every 100 ml and the new one 120 mg, so a 15 ml spoonful of the usual gravy is 88.5 mg against 18.0 mg of the new one - nearly five times as much - and that difference of about 70.5 mg is what the panel was being asked to find. They found it: cup A was named as the saltier one by 10 of the 12 panellists, 1 named B and 1 could not tell. Their saltiness scores say the same thing in numbers: A averages 4.42 out of 5, which is the band the score sheet labels 'far too salty', and B averages 2.83, which is the band labelled 'a little salt'. The acceptability scores are the result that decided the project. Cup A averages 2.58 and cup B 4.33, and 11 of the 12 panellists said they would eat the new one again against 1 who preferred the usual gravy. The one who preferred the usual gravy wrote on the score sheet that the new one 'tastes like food, not like Sunday', which is worth recording rather than smoothing over: one person in twelve missed the salt, and the taste of the household's own cooking is a real thing that a plan can take away. But the twelve scores together say what the household needed to hear, which is that a gravy with a fifth of the sodium in it can still be the one that most people would choose. What the panel could not judge is the whole plate: they tasted the two gravies on their own, out of cups, without the chicken, the rice and the vegetables they were made for, and a gravy tasted alone always shows its salt more than a gravy poured over a dinner does.

pages.heading: Practical results: the tasting panel's scores for the dinner
pages.body: After the two gravies had been tasted, the panel scored the dinner itself on five attributes, from 1 to 5, on a score sheet that named the middle of the scale before they began. The dinner averages between 4.08 and 4.50 on all five attributes, which is a good result for a meal with 558.3 mg of sodium a portion, and the pattern inside the five scores is the interesting part rather than the averages. Appearance and overall acceptability both score 4.50, which says that the plate did not look like a meal with something missing from it; aroma scores 4.33, carried by the pimento and the thyme; and texture scores 4.42 because the chicken was baked on the bone and the rice was cooked with a lid on. Taste is the lowest of the five at 4.08, which is exactly what should be expected and is the score the folder pays most attention to: salt is a taste and not a look or a smell, so if the panel were going to miss anything it would be the taste of the food, and two panellists asked for salt before they were halfway through their portion. The comments on the score sheets are more useful than the numbers, and the ones that changed the plan are these: the pimento and the thyme were named by six panellists as what they noticed first; two asked for salt; one said the vegetables 'tasted green, in a good way'; and three said the pumpkin and carrot mash would be better with more pepper. The suggestion that went into the folder's improvement list came from my brother, who was not on the panel: he wanted ketchup on his rice, and the household's answer was the lime and the tomato that were already on the table instead. What the panel could not judge is how the dinner tastes on its fifth day, and that is a real limitation: a plan that is eaten once is a recipe, not a week, and the household's own verdict on the whole week - my father's words were that he stopped noticing after the third day - is a different and softer test than a panel's score sheet.

pages.body: At the end of the planned week the market list was added up against the five heads of the budget, and the result is in the table: J$23,989.00 spent of the J$25,300.00 set aside, leaving J$1,311.00, and every head under its own figure. The comparison with the week before the project is the number my mother wanted to see, because she was the one who said the vegetables were never the problem. The household's receipts for the week before the project come to J$26,892.28 priced with the same price list, which is J$1,592.28 more than the household wanted to spend and J$2,903.28 more than the planned week, so the healthier week is also the cheaper week by 10.8 per cent. Where did that money come from? Not from the vegetables, which went up by J$722.50 on the practical dinner alone, and not from the fruit. It came from four lines that are not in the new list at all: the ready-cut and seasoned chicken, which the whole birds bought at the market replace; the corned beef; the sweet drinks; and the biscuits and snacks, which came to J$1,500.00 a week in the old basket. My mother's reading of it, which the folder agrees with, is that the household was paying for salt and sugar in convenient packaging, and the plan moved that money on to food. The leftovers record belongs in this section too, because a budget that is met by throwing food away is not met. Nothing was thrown away in the planned week: the chicken bones and wing tips from the four birds made about two litres of stock, which the rice and the pumpkin soup were cooked in; the portion of dinner left over on Wednesday went into Thursday's lunch; the callaloo left on Monday went into Wednesday's lunch in the bread; and the unused 1 g of the day's salt stayed in the tin. The one thing that was bought and not used was the ketchup, which came off the table after the first week, and it is in the cupboard now rather than in the bin.

pages.heading: Discussion: why the sodium fell and what carried the flavour
pages.body: The sodium fell for four reasons and only the first of them is the salt tin. The first is the salt itself: the household's cooking went from about 20.6 g of salt a day to about 5.7 g, which is 144 g in the old week against 40 g in the planned one, and because salt is about 40 per cent sodium and the household is four people, that change alone moves each person's day by 2,057 mg down to 571 mg. The second reason is the seasoning cube, which is the one item in the cupboard that surprised everybody: one cube a day put 275 mg of sodium into each of our plates, which is more than everything the plan now adds to a dinner pot. The third is the salt that arrives in food somebody else seasoned - the pre-seasoned chicken from the supermarket and the patties and the corned beef - and the fourth is the table itself, the ketchup bottle that my brother reached for every day before the plan and that the household took off the table. Put together they take the week from 27,875.0 mg of sodium for each of us to 11,852.5, a fall of 16,022.5 mg a week or 2,288.9 mg a day, which is 57.5 per cent. What is much harder to answer is the question my mother asked at the start: if the salt comes out, what is left? The panel's scores in section 19 are the evidence that something was left. Salt does three jobs in a pot of Jamaican food - it makes the food taste seasoned, it pushes the flavours of the other ingredients forward, and it hides the smell of meat - and each of those jobs was given to something else in this plan. Garlic, ginger, pimento, thyme and black pepper make the food taste seasoned; lime and tomato make it taste bright and fresh and let the vegetables taste of themselves; and the lime and the long rub and the browning take care of the smell of the chicken. The one job nothing replaced is the mouth-feel of salt on its own, which is what the two panellists who asked for salt were missing and what the panellist who said the new gravy 'tastes like food, not like Sunday' was describing. That is a real loss and the folder does not pretend otherwise. The potassium is worth a line as well, because it is the other half of the story: the practical dinner carried 1,869 mg of potassium for each of us from the peas, the callaloo, the pumpkin, the carrot, the pawpaw and the yoghurt, the food tables show, and potassium is the mineral that works against sodium in the body. The nurse was told about that figure, and it is the reason the plan is not offered as a pattern for anybody with kidney disease, where a high potassium intake has to be decided by a doctor and not by a school project.

pages.heading: Discussion: the taste, the time and the money against the plan
pages.body: The hypothesis had three parts - the sodium would fall by more than half, the family would still eat the food, and the week would cost no more than the budget - and the honest verdict is that two and a half of them held. The sodium fell by 57.5 per cent, from 3,982.1 mg a day for each of us to 1,693.2, so that part held with room to spare, and it held on a counting method that is deliberately conservative, because it leaves out the sodium that fresh food carries. The food was eaten and liked: the dinner scored 4.50 for overall acceptability, only taste came below 4.33, and my father's own verdict was that he stopped noticing the change after the third day. The budget held - J$23,989.00 spent of J$25,300.00 - but the hypothesis said the week would cost no more than the budget, and the honest word for that is 'passed', not 'better', because the week does not come in under the old week's spending without the four lines that were dropped; the vegetables and the fruit by themselves cost more than the food they replaced. The half that did not hold is the widest claim in the hypothesis and the one the week actually tested: that the household's day would stay inside 1,500 mg. It does not on three days of seven. Friday fails on 20 g of cheese, Saturday on one patty bought at the sports day, and Sunday on the ackee and salted fish, which by itself is more than the whole target. The plan's own verdict therefore is that the kitchen half of the change was achieved and the two places it fails are both outside the kitchen: the food bought on the road and a traditional Sunday dish that the household will not give up. That is a more useful result than a clean win would have been, because it says where the next change has to happen. The time plan is the smallest failure in the folder and the most instructive: 13 minutes over a plan of 155, and the largest single cause is a sandy bunch of callaloo and a pumpkin nobody weighed before buying it. None of the twelve stages was mis-ordered and nothing was cooked late, so the failure is not the order of work but the assumption that a market vegetable matches the weight in the recipe - a lesson worth more than the 13 minutes it cost.

pages.heading: Limitations and improvements
pages.body: A folder that claims a perfect week is not telling the truth, and the limits below are the ones the project actually ran into. They are grouped in the order of how much they matter to the results above. The first three are about the sodium figures, because those are the numbers the whole project stands on, and the ones after that are about the cooking, the money and the work itself.
bullets: The counting method cannot see the sodium that fresh food carries. The day-to-day table counts the weighed salt and the label figures, and section 16 shows that for the practical dinner it leaves out 195.8 mg a portion. Improvement: weigh and count one whole day every month ingredient by ingredient, the way the dinner was counted, and keep the other six days on the simple count.

The salted fish is an assumption and not a measurement. The label figure is for the fish as it is sold and the folder counts half of it after soaking and boiling; nobody measured how much comes out. Improvement: ask a laboratory at the college or the health centre what a soaked sample actually carries, or replace the salted fish with fresh fish, which the food tables put at about 90 mg of sodium in 100 g.

The salt tin measures the salt and not the food. The pack was weighed and the menu adds up to the same figure, but the weight tells us how much left the tin, not how much reached each plate; a pot of food shared unevenly spreads its salt unevenly. Improvement: serve the grain and the peas with a measuring cup for one week and weigh the portions, as the practical dinner did.

Three of the seven days are over the household's own 1,500 mg target, and two of the three are caused by food bought away from home. Improvement: carry a packed lunch on the sports day instead of buying the patty, which alone is 700 mg, and move the cheese to the days without a patty.

Sunday's ackee and salted fish cannot fit inside the target at any portion the household would call a portion. Improvement: keep it as a fortnightly breakfast with the portion cut to 25 g, and use fresh fish on the other Sundays; the folder works out in section 24 that this one change brings the week's average inside the target.

The ketchup came off the table only after the first week, so four of the planned days still carry 165 mg for it. Improvement: keep the bottle off the table from the start and put the lime and the tomato on instead, which is what the household now does.

The panel tasted the gravies alone and the dinner once. A gravy tasted on its own shows its salt more than a gravy poured over rice, and a meal eaten once is not the same as a meal eaten on the fifth day. Improvement: taste the two gravies a second time poured over the same rice, and ask the household to score the plan at the end of the week as well as a panel at the start.

The time plan assumed the market vegetables matched the weights in the recipes. The pumpkin was larger and the callaloo was sandy, which cost 5 minutes at the busiest stage. Improvement: weigh the pumpkin at the market and wash and pick over the callaloo at home the night before.

The two school scales differed by 5 g in a 500 g bag of rice, so every weight was taken twice on the kitchen scale. Improvement: check the class scales against a known weight at the start of the session, the way the bag of rice was used here, and write the correction on the board.

One price list was used for every comparison in the folder, which makes the comparisons fair but makes the money figures a snapshot. Tomato and sweet pepper had already moved between the survey and the shopping trip. Improvement: price the list twice, a fortnight apart, and report the plan against the higher of the two.

pages.heading: Conclusion
pages.body: The project set out to find out whether a household that includes a man with high blood pressure could eat a week of the food it likes with far less salt, on the money it can actually set aside. It can. The week was planned to the five rules the family agreed, cooked, eaten and counted, and the result is that the sodium in each person's day fell from 3,982.1 mg to 1,693.2 mg - 57.5 per cent lower - while the food was still eaten, and the week cost J$23,989.00 of the J$25,300.00 the household set aside, which is J$2,903.28 less than the week the family was spending before the project started. The sodium fell for four reasons that can each be pointed at: 144 g of salt a week became 40 g; the seasoning cube came out of the pot and took 275 mg a plate a day with it; the pre-seasoned chicken, the corned beef and the tinned meat left the basket; and the ketchup came off the table. What carried the flavour instead was garlic, ginger, pimento, thyme, escallion, black pepper, lime and tomato, and the evidence that they worked is the blind tasting: 11 of 12 panellists said they would eat the new gravy again, and they scored it 4.33 for acceptability against 2.58 for the gravy the household used to make. The same tasting found the limit of the change too: one panellist preferred the old gravy, and two asked for salt before they finished the plate, which is the honest size of what is lost when the salt comes out. What the project did not manage is as clear as what it did. The household's own target of 1,500 mg a day is not met on Friday, Saturday or Sunday, and the two biggest causes sit outside the kitchen: one patty bought at the sports day and one traditional Sunday breakfast of ackee and salted fish, which alone carries 1,600 mg counted at half the label. Working the week's figures through the improvements in section 23 shows how little it takes to close the gap: replacing the salted fish with fresh fish takes the average to 1,478 mg a day, taking the ketchup off the table as well takes it to 1,383, and carrying a packed lunch on the sports day instead of buying the patty takes it to 1,283 mg, which is inside the target on every one of the seven days, and none of those three changes needs money or a special ingredient. The household has kept two of the changes since the week ended - the seasoning cube is out of the pot and the ketchup is off the table - and my mother's own summing up was that the food costs less when you stop buying salt in packets. If I were to take this project on again I would count one full day ingredient by ingredient every week rather than only the practical dinner, weigh the market vegetables before buying them, and ask the panel to taste the gravies poured over rice rather than out of a cup, because those three changes would make the figures in this folder harder to argue with.

pages.heading: Sources and acknowledgements
pages.body: The sources below are the ones actually used in this project, and the notes say plainly which figures are working values rather than measurements. Every person, household, shop, price, panel and food figure in this folder is invented for this worked example: the Reid household, Sample Village, the shops named in section 5, the twelve panellists and all the weights, prices, times and scores describe nothing real, and the folder is a school assignment and not medical advice to anybody. No part of the CSEC syllabus or of any published examiner's report is reproduced here; the guide's own task list is used to check that the folder answers every task it is marked against.
bullets: The CSEC Food and Nutrition syllabus and the SBA guide: the theme-and-research, planning, preparation, practical and evaluation tasks, and the 50 marks they carry in our guide
The class food composition tables: the working values used for sodium, energy, protein, potassium and fibre in this folder, applied to the weights as served rather than raw
The World Health Organization's advice to adults on salt: less than 5 g of salt, about 2,000 mg of sodium, a day, which the household's usual week was running at about double

The conversion used throughout: salt is about 40 per cent sodium by weight, so 1 g of salt carries about 400 mg of sodium, and the salt in a portion is about two and a half times the sodium figure on the label

The pack labels read in the cupboard: bread, margarine, ketchup, the seasoning cube, browning, tinned mackerel, corned beef, cheese, milk, yoghurt, the patty and the salted cod, each figure quoted with the item it came from

The clinic's advice to my father and the household's own working target, set with the nurse and written down before the week started; the project is not medical advice and a person with kidney disease must ask a doctor before copying a plan high in fruit, peas and green vegetables

Thanks to my mother for keeping the receipts and the salt tin honest, to my father for eating the week and saying that he stopped noticing, to my brother for the ketchup complaint that went into the improvements, to the twelve panellists who tasted blind, and to my teacher for coding the cups and never hinting at which one was which

examinerNotes: This subject is marked out of 50 under six tasks, and the folder answers each one with real work: a theme taken from the household's own kitchen, twelve labels read, a three-shop survey, a budget split into five heads, a seven-day menu with five written rules, recipes with quantities and reasons, a costed market list, a twelve-stage time plan run against the clock, a practical dinner weighed ingredient by ingredient, a blind tasting with twelve panellists, and an evaluation that keeps its own score honest.

The strongest feature is that the folder counts. 1 g of salt is 400 mg of sodium; 144 g of salt a week becomes 27,875.0 mg for each of the four of us and 40 g becomes 11,852.5; the same 3 g of salt in the practical pot is 1,200 mg in a pot that measures 2,233.1 mg altogether; the gravies are 590 mg and 120 mg a 100 ml because the seasoning in each litre is known to the gram. Every figure in the folder was derived from one set of weights, one food table and one price list, so no table contradicts another.

The research method is worth copying: the salt tin was weighed at the start and the end of both weeks, which turns 'we use a lot of salt' into 144 g and 40 g; the seasoning cube was counted from how long a pack of twenty lasts; and the labels were read and turned into portion figures rather than left as figures per 100 g. The three-shop survey prices the same 4.2 kg a week in each shop, so the saving of J$1,260.00 a week on the chicken is a real week and not a price on a board.

The blind comparison is set up properly: two litres of gravy from the same base chicken, seasoned one the household's usual way and one the new way, so the seasoning is the only variable; coded cups, 10 ml each, water between, saltiness and acceptability scored separately. 11 of 12 panellists chose the new gravy and the cup with five times the sodium in it was named correctly by most of them - which is why the score sheet is evidence and not opinion.

The evaluation earns its marks by keeping its failures: three of the seven days are over the household's own 1,500 mg target, the salted fish is counted at half its label figure and the assumption is written down as one, the day-to-day count is shown to miss the sodium naturally in fresh food by 195.8 mg a portion, and the reworked dinner is admitted to cost J$89.36 more for four portions than the meal it replaced. The improvements then work the arithmetic forward to show what would close the gap rather than just hoping.

Everything here is invented for this worked example: the household, Sample Village, the shops, the prices, the panel and every weight, cost and score. It is a school assignment and not medical advice - a person with kidney disease in particular must ask a doctor before following a plan that raises the fruit, peas and green vegetables in the diet. Cook your own week for your own household, with your own weights, your own labels and your own panel.
